utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, were -- all the reports from the HQ were actually second-hand reports? First-hand reports came from the observers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness already answered this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please now have 65 ter 9837.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a report from the UNMO Sarajevo Sector, from Captain Hansen, who prepared it, Captain Hansen, and it was issued by Colonel Alam? And you can see here in the first paragraph where it says "the 28th of June, at 9.20," and it is being described here. Is it here a description of that event?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen this report before. It's like an immediate report, it's dated the 29th of June. And I read this report, and I have no information about why or how it's made like this. And it's not up to me to say anything about what this report is stating. I only know what I saw the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you report? Why isn't there your part, the part that you reported, in this report? There is another part of the text towards the bottom of the page here, where it says: "Another UNMO was on the parking place at the same time, and his report is included." So why isn't your report from OP 4 part of this report as well? Do you have an explanation? Did you report to your HQ what you saw?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why not my report is included in this report of the 29th of June. I reported orally, as far as I know, directly to the OP -- to the UN HQ the same day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page here of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that it says here that the team, your team from OP 4 that was looking into that area, was taking cover, and there is no report from them? There is no information from that observation post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was written, but it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, am I supposed to take your word for it that you submitted an oral report, whereas we have an official document, a report from Captain Hansen and Colonel Alam, about there being no report from you? So in what way and how did you submit your report on this matter, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was raising to make the point that the witness -- Mr. Karadzic is being argumentative, and he should simply put his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness is able to answer this question. Can you? Can you answer the question, Mr. Brennskag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have my word, yes, because I'm under oath. I don't know why my oral report is not attached to this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that the report is usually submitted by the leader of the monitoring team; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that normally, usually, it was submitted, a daily report from the UNMO team, yes. These events, the 28th of June, was special, so we were going directly with our oral report to HQ, UNMO HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that written reports were submitted about less important events, while oral reports were submitted about important events? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that normally we made written reports. At that time, we also used oral reports because it was so much that happened that sometimes we had to go directly to the HQ with our reports. Normally, we also used radio reports, but at this time we didn't dare because of our own safety. And I have stated before that when we reported such happenings -- such events on the radio, we were fired at from the BiH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that unimportant events were reported on by the team leader, whereas important events were reported on by his colleague, who was not a team leader and was not a senior team member; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Brennskag: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has answered the question about what was important and unimportant and what was reported and what wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. If you find it impossible to conclude by 12.30, we need to take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have more time, really. I've seen that in other cases, greater faith was given to this unreliable recollection than to this reliable document. I cannot leave that unclarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not a necessary statement, and unhelpful. And think about the time wasted in relation to the witness this morning, as I indicated earlier on. I think you should be able to finish your cross-examination by 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, I would ask you, if you respond to me with a yes or no, then we will finish more quickly. Were you the team leader that day or not?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never team leader in the Pofalici team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the team leader submitted reports?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Normally, I said, the team leader submitted reports every day. That's because the team had several tasks. The team had the OP, they had investigations, and they had patrols when they were able to do the patrols.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I please have the first page of this document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that it says here that this was fired from the B and H Army territory and that that is approximately 1800 metres from the nearest confrontation line? Yes or no; does it say that or not?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read what is stated, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we get the last page. The last page is the diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the original, is this the diagram that accompanies the telegram and states that the bomb was 60 centimetres wide, that it had fins, and that it looked like this?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if this sketch were -- supported the report, and I don't know who was drawing it, and I don't have -- I have never seen such a bomb, so I have no idea what's written here about which bomb it is, and the size of it, and how it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is 612, 613, and 614. Those are the page numbers, so it's a part of this telegram. Did you know that the Muslim side was modifying air-bombs?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: To your question about the ABiH and modified air-bombs, I did not know that they had such air-bombs, and I don't know today if they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you cannot rule it out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D853, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D2680, please. We are just going to look at this briefly, one paragraph. 1D2680, yes. I don't know if there's a translation. Allow me to inform you about the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Command of the 12th Division, strictly confidential, Sarajevo, the 23rd of June [as interpreted], 1995: "Fortification of firing position and PVO positions for striking at targets on the ground, to be delivered to the unit commands."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think the document is dated the 23rd of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I said "July," but I probably didn't articulate enough. Allow me to read it, just the first paragraph: "Touring the units of the 12th Division, it was established that the firing positions for the PVO weapons, used to shoot at surface targets, have not been properly executed. In order to improve the state of the same, I order: Firing positions that have been constructed in order to strike at targets on the surface need to be additionally constructed, fortified up to a sufficient degree to guarantee the safety of the operators and enable long-term firing. While carrying out the engineering works on the firing positions, pay attention to complete masking ..." And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it clear to you now why you didn't see their installations, because they had masked them very well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about -- I didn't have and I don't have any knowledge about that they had those kind of improvised air-bombs on the ABiH side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, you know the position of the Chamber, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this speaks about the same thing that the UN observer should have known about, because he was observing what the parties to the conflict were doing. This is a document by the Muslim party, proving that they did have them, and it corresponds with what Captain Hansen said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He commented about his knowledge of a modified bomb on the part of the Muslim side, and he commented on the UNMO report. That's all you can get from this witness. You will have another opportunity to tender this document later on, and you can make a submission as to his credibility or not, or anything else. It is just totally a waste of time putting these kind of documents to the witness, who knows nothing about this. And you can't complain shortage of your time. You have 15 minutes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, did you know that from the Sarajevo Television building, fire was opened at us using artillery weapons? Did you know that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never knew that it was firing from the television building.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 09850. 09850.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is information about the situation at the front. This is not a report. It's information. Let's see what the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was reporting on the 30th of June, 1995. May I -- the first sentence is: "The Muslim offensive to raise the blockade of Sarajevo that has been in progress for 15 days." The third paragraph: "Due to the lack of success and enormous losses in their ranks, the enemy artillery is fiercely attacking along the entire front-line and at inhabited areas." In the middle of this paragraph, it says: "Our artillery is precisely responding to the fire by the Muslim artillery attacks. In one such response on the 28th of June, they hit the Radio/Television Centre of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Mr. Brennskag, does it not state here that -- does it state here that the strike was an artillery strike or an air-bomb strike?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see what's written, and I only can say what I saw. And it was an air-bomb that I could trace, and just afterwards it was an explosion in the TV building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you have seen an artillery shell?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an artillery shell on its way to -- to the goal or to the -- where it's aimed, it could scarcely -- maybe you are happy to see it, but I never saw it in Sarajevo. I've seen it in my training at home in Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Brennskag, that you would see the smoke immediately upon firing, and it would be visible from 1.7 to 4 seconds, at the most? Did you know that? And then after that, there is no smoke tail that is visible?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what I saw. I saw the smoke tail, and I can't say for how many seconds I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, you saw what Mr. Hansen saw as well, that the Muslims fired that shell - who knows where it was directed at - and you did not see the Serb artillery shell because it was not visible. Can we tender this document? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I didn't saw what Mr. Hansen saw.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, we'll --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D854, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that the opposing side is happy. They probably wanted to offer that in the redirect, but this is a document speaking about the artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, were you informed about the incident in Geteova Street, in the Alipasino neighbourhood, on the 22nd of June, 1995? You said at the time that one girl was killed.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the 22nd of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, he said "22nd."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- June, and I was not only informed; I was asked to go there immediate to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you say that in your diary?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no answer to that. It's my private diary or written memories. That's open for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were not permitted to go to the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we were not admitted to go to the hospital. Or if there was someone else from the team that should go there, I don't remember, but I was not in the hospital -- at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were not able to decide from which point the projectile was fired; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we couldn't exactly tell the point of firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were not able to explain how fragments or shrapnel of the projectile killed anyone who was positioned behind some kind of barrier or some kind of wall?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my knowledge. We just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You stated this in your testimony in the case of General Milosevic on the 8th of March, on page 3497. Now we're wasting time on this, but can shrapnel like that kill someone who is behind the wall?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I think I said then, it will be speculations. We investigated the impact on the pavement, and we registrated [sic] that one girl was taken away from the spot. She was seriously wounded. I saw her face, and I thought she were killed. And afterwards, not me, but others in the UN could state that she was dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was she at the point in time the explosion went off?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there where the explosion -- where the impact or the explosion went off, and that's why I don't know where she was exactly at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you did not show the condition of the wall and the effects of the explosion on the wall?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I did not. As far as I know, our report was from the investigation of the impact in -- on the pavement, and from what has happened -- what we saw on the pavement, we were able to trace from which direction the projectile has been fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you expect to find traces of fragments on the nearby wall? Where did those fragments disappear to? There had to have been some traces on the wall; right?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, I don't want to speculate on. I can't remember that we investigated traces on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said in the Milosevic case, 3498, page 3498 - it's not in front of me - you said that you did not investigate the condition of the wall. Can we now look at 1D2691, please, and the parties can look at that page. And can we have 1D2691. Are you asserting that this was a civilian zone, without military targets?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the projectile impacted, I went -- from my investigation at the spot, I couldn't see any military compounds or -- but, of course, I didn't investigate all the area around. So up to my knowledge, I didn't see any military positions at the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a combat report, dated 30th of June, i.e., eight days after the incident, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 1st Corps Command. Can we now have page 2. The second paragraph, "State of Security," it reads: "On the 29th of June, 1995, from the debris of the building on 5 Cetinjska Street that had previously been hit by a modified air-bomb, a dead body of a member of the 142nd Croatian Light Brigade, Slavko Lovric, was extracted." Do you agree that Cetinjska and Geteova Streets were actually one-and-the-same street? I would direct the parties to look at Table G-6, in which Geteova Street is marked as "Cetinjska Street" in the summary. Did you know that seven days after the explosion we mentioned before, a body of a killed soldier was pulled out?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I don't know the name of the streets. And I don't know that -- what's stated here, that a body was taken out eight days after the 22nd of June. I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you accept now that there was something of a military nature there?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would only be speculations, and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you deal with the incident on Zadarska Street, which took place on the 1st of July, 1995? But before that, can we have this document admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think the witness has added anything to this document, and it's -- and for that reason, I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's no basis, Mr. Karadzic, to admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document directly disputes the fact that this was a civilian zone, and this document was produced by the Muslim Army. How can I challenge this witness if I'm not able to challenge this same subject? And this document does that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you put your question to the witness, who denied -- who couldn't confirm what you are saying, but you have ample opportunity to tender this document. It's purely a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you deal with the incident -- Your Excellency, I truly and really need another 15 minutes. Did you deal with the incident on Zadarska Street?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, how much would you need for your redirect, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Five to ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break for 10 minutes now, and so we'll resume at quarter to 1:00. Then you will have 10 minutes to conclude your cross-examination, and the Prosecution will have 5 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are going to take a break, why can't I be given more time, let's say half an hour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we can't go longer than one hour for the morning of today. We'll have a break for 10 minutes now. We'll resume at quarter to 1.00. --- Break taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you remember the Zadarska Street incident of the 1st of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was investigating this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You reached a conclusion regarding the direction from which the shot came, but you didn't establish the distance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you concluded that it might have come six or seven kilometres from the point of impact, from the direction north/north-east; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I concluded that the direction was from north/north-east, but not the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So no conclusion could have been reached about the distance. Thank you. Do you remember the Marko Oreskovic Street incident which took place on the 18th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not investigating any incident the 18th of June, as far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the previous one on Zadarska Street was not the incident mentioned in your diary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I don't know what was in my private diary, but I think I didn't mention either the -- no, I didn't mention the Zadarska Street, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 14731.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting: Mr. Brennskag, you testified about the incident on Marko Oreskovic Street of the 18th of June, 1995, and you concluded that - and that was in your testimony in the Perisic case on the 9th of February, 2009, on page 3375 - that there was fighting going on, that there were several explosions, and that it was impossible for you to conclude the origin of the shell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if I testified about the incident on Marko Oreskovic Street on the 18th of June. For sure, I did not investigate it. Then, there was a lot of firing going on in that area, yes, and sometimes it was not possible to conclude the origin of shells. But we have to go -- then go to the reports from UN OPs to be correct -- from UN HQ -- UN Observer HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it was 1146. This is what you testified on page 3375 on the 19th of February, 1113, then 1149, 1250, 1305. So there were a lot of shells, and that was a proper fighting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't have these pages in front of me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had time, I would like to call up 8186 to show you that that was a report produced by your service, but I don't have the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Since it's in evidence, can we then look at the next page in your diary. I'm going to read it. [In English] "In order for an UNMO unit to be able to function according to its mandate, there must, in my view, be a definite cease-fire arrangement in place between the conflicting parties." [Interpretation] So it's paragraph 4, first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my view, to do a good job as UN observers, yes, but I say "in my view."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last sentence: [In English] "On top of that, in certain situations I had the feeling that the neutral party was not always that neutral." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's written like this, but I can't confirm it. I have no exact information about it. It's my thoughts in my private writings. That's open for the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 10. Page 10: [In English] "I begin to perceive that some of my fellow observers from certain NATO countries are engaged in a completely different assignment to the one which was envisaged. Trust in the observers is beginning to crumble."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that your position and your feeling at the time?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my feeling at that time, and it's not -- I'm not able to verify it. But it's written like this in my open diary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see where it says: "On the 15th of June --" [In English] "June 15th, the BH starts an offensive to break the siege of Sarajevo. The offensive gradually peters out, and the BSA intensifies its bombardment of Sarajevo and other so-called safe areas." [Interpretation] Would you be surprised if I showed you, if I had time, the consumption of artillery and ammunition and explosions by the Muslim Army? They used 1.000, 2.000 and 3.000 more rounds than the Serbian Army. Would you accept this as a possible assertion that the Muslim side actually fired many more projectiles than --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is calling for the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, was it possible that there was some firing from the Muslim side that you failed to register?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I talked about it earlier, but of course it's possible that we missed the fire -- some firing from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please focus now on the end of the first paragraph: [In English] "Immediately after NATO carries out extensive air-strikes against strategic targets in Bosnian Serb areas, I stand as a spectator in the old town and watch as the planes come in and drop their bomb loads around Sarajevo. At last, the international community has shown that it is serious about something it has said. At last, Sarajevo's pain will soon be over. In truth, it was a peace that was dearly bought." [Interpretation] So you accuse others of being biased, but it seems that you, yourself, were, to a certain extent, against the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not written like this. It's written, what is stated, when it happened, when the NATO started their bombardment. So no to your question, it was not against the Serbian side, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brennskag. I take it that was your last question. Ms. Sutherland --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to say I'm not happy with the time allocated to me. I did not ask enough questions of this witness, and I would like to state this for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll not repeat what we said. It is for you, how to plan your cross-examination. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was going to say while we have this document on the screen, if we could just go to page 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, it was put to you at page 64 and a little earlier today that you didn't note specifically, in your personal notes, reference to the incidents that you investigated on the 22nd of June, 1995, and the 1st of July, 1995. In your personal notes, though, did you put, in general terms, the tasks that you were to undertake as a UN military observer?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not a formal document, and most of the tasks were not taken in this document because this I remember by my heart. This is just a document to know a little bit more what happened around me at that time, because when I was there at the spot in June/July, we didn't know that much what happened around us, in the big view.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we take a look at the second paragraph on top of page 10, it states there that you did follow-up investigations of bombing, and "injuries and deaths as a result of bombardments in Sarajevo are traumatic and wear down every member of the team." So that was the extent of what you put in your personal diary. Did you tell the Office of the Prosecutor, though, when you were interviewed in May 1996, about these two incidents?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1996, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can turn now to another topic. If I could have Exhibit D853 on the screen. This is the special report written by Captain Hansen. And if we could go to the last page. Sorry, second-to-last page. It says there: "The UNMO team that normally man OP 4 that looks into the area was taking cover in the shelter because of shelling at the time of the incident, so no information is available from the OP."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was there a shelter within OP 4 that you went to on that day, on the 28th of June, 1995, when you witnessed the modified air-bomb from Ilidza hitting the TV building?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building we had at OP 4 was a civilian accommodation, a house, and there were no built-up shelters, as that, in the house. But the house had a basement that were normally used by those who lived there. It was a couple. When it was tense, they lived in the basement. I was there once or twice to visit them, to talk to them, socialise, but I was never in that basement to take cover, myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Thank you, Mr. Brennskag. That concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised that we need to start the afternoon session at 2.30 so that the Registry could have some time to check the effectiveness of the videolink. And is there anything -- there's one matter I'd like to deal with now, which relates to the modification of protective measurements as regards KDZ477 and 485. We dealt with Miokovic. So in the absence of the consent of the witness, a variation of protective measures can only be ordered in exceptional circumstances. According to the Prosecution responses, both of the witnesses have not agreed to any variation of their protective measures. Having considered the reason provided by the witnesses, the Chamber finds there are no exceptional circumstances which would testify -- which, I'm sorry, would justify modification of the protective measures granted by the earlier Chambers. I also consulted the Judges related to the earlier cases, who were all in agreement with this decision. Therefore, the motion is therefore denied. So we will resume with the videolink at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.09 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Good afternoon, Madam Mujanovic. Thank you for appearing before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could kindly take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean aloud?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we were not able to hear you. Could you read that aloud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking: Am I to read it aloud?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mujanovic. You will be asked some questions by the Prosecution, and afterwards by the accused, Mr. Karadzic. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Mujanovic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As we discussed on the telephone the other day, can you please let the Presiding Judge know at any time if you need to have a break. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Fahra Mujanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in November 2008; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've had an opportunity to review this statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could 65 ter 22567 be put on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, that statement that you see in front of you, do you recognise that as the statement that was taken from you on the 5th of November, 2008? Mr. Registrar, it's behind tab 22567.

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does that statement accurately reflect what you said at that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you were examined in court today on the same matters contained in that statement, would you provide the same information to the Court in response to questions about those matters?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender for admission 65 ter 22567, the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1865, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And with the Court's permission, I'll read a short summary of the evidence contained in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The witness lived with her husband and children in the Barica settlement, which is located in a valley between the elevations of Zuc and Poljine, to the north of the city of Sarajevo. From early April 1992, the Barica settlement was subjected to shelling and sniping coming from the Bosnian Serb military positions which had been established on the hills and commanding positions around the settlement, from Zuc, Krivoglavci, Kromolj, Vogosca, Poljine and Tihovici. The witness learnt that some of the shell fire was from weapons known as a Praga, a three-barrelled anti-aircraft machine-gun, and a multiple rocket-launcher known as VBR. Mrs. Mujanovic left the family house for around 20 days or so because of the shelling, but had to return to Barica due to over-crowding in the house she and her family had sought refuge. On their return to Barica, the shelling and sniping continued. On the 8th of June, 1992, Mrs. Mujanovic was injured at her residential home in Barica by shrapnel from an 88-millimetre mortar shell when it exploded between her house and her neighbour's house. No one came to her assistance immediately because the shelling continued and people were afraid to approach her in case they were hit. The witness was driven to the Kosevo Hospital, where she was admitted and operated on. However, many pieces of shrapnel were not removed from her body. She was hospitalised for a period of 12 days. The day that Mrs. Mujanovic was wounded and hospitalised, there were about 150 other persons wounded because of shelling that occurred throughout Sarajevo. Mrs. Mujanovic describes the trauma suffered as a result of the shelling and sniping, and the physical and psychological effects upon her. That concludes the brief summary of the witness's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, I want to ask you just a few questions now. How far is the settlement of Barica from Sarajevo, as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not much. I wouldn't know how far. I'm not good at that sort of reckoning. It's not far.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate approximately how many kilometres?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Two or three kilometres. I'm not sure. If you go on foot, it's about 20 minutes, maybe even less.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is the settlement a residential one?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the town?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. What was the settlement made up of, predominantly? Was it a residential settlement?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a residential neighbourhood where I lived. There's nothing but residences, civilian houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraphs 7 and 8 of Exhibit P1865, which is your statement now in evidence, you state that from the early part of 1992, the area where you resided was subject to shelling and sniping. What was the intensity of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes in one day, more than a thousand shells would fall on the neighbourhood and around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You stated, in paragraph 6, that the shelling and sniping occurred from the positions on the hills and around the settlement, and those were the places that I just read out in the summary of your evidence: Zuc, Krivoglavci - I'm sorry for my translation - Kromolj, Vogosca, Poljine --

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- Tihovici?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You state that they were held by Bosnian Serb forces. How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Because the civilian population had been driven out of that. Only they remained there, and that's where the fire onto our neighbourhood came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "only they remained there," can you specify particularly who you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim population was driven out of there, but many were killed as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, a moment ago you said "only they remained there." Can you specify exactly who you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Mujanovic, do you hear me now? The Registrar will take a look into the matter. Mrs. Mujanovic, do you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I'll call to the technician and have him come in and fix this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it now you are able to follow me. Mrs. Mujanovic, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear a thing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No, obviously she's still having problems hearing you. I'll call the technician and have him fix the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you like to deal with some small matters while we're waiting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, do you hear me? While the technicians will take a look into the matter, we will deal with some administrative matters. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I spoke with Dr. Karadzic and other members of our team, and we're now in a position to agree to hear the testimony of Witness KDZ485 on Wednesday. So we'll do our best. But it's difficult for us, but under the circumstances, we're willing to make the best effort we can to accommodate that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your co-operation. And you must have heard by now that three hours and a half --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we received --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, the technician is on the way. He should be here in a minute to fix the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We didn't -- I don't believe Dr. Karadzic has received that yet, but I did receive an e-mail indicating that the Chamber has allocated three and a half hours for his cross-examination. I don't know whether that will be enough, but at least if he starts on Wednesday, we can make accommodations to hear him for longer and before the end of the week, if necessary. Also, Mr. President, just to let you know, we don't oppose the Prosecution's motion filed today concerning leave to reply for the judicial notice of intercepts. We won't be filing any written response to that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that. That is granted, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And also, Mr. President, we would ask that the Chamber and the Prosecution try to quickly resolve the issue of the witness Charles Kirudja, who is scheduled to be heard during the third week of November and who we strenuously object to hearing out of order. So that if it's necessary that he's going to testify, then we can at least start whatever inadequate preparations we're going to able to make. But we would really appreciate it if the Chamber and the Prosecutor would not burden us with that job. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider the matter. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe we should be able to file our response no later than tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] it should be okay now. Can you tell the Trial Chamber that it should be okay now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, do you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Great. Ms. Sutherland from the Prosecution will continue to ask more questions. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, a moment ago you said that Muslims were driven out of the areas that you mentioned, and you said that "they remained there." Who, in particular, are you referring to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs remained there, and the Muslim people were driven out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So do I understand you well to say that you were not able to physically go to these positions where you saw the shells being fired from?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Never. We didn't dare to walk around our own houses, let alone go there --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What weapons did you see, in particular?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw a tank at Tihovici, in the middle of a field.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you witness any mortar and sniper fire coming from any other directions?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know the Pretis factory in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know, I know that. And from there, too, they fired upon our neighbourhood. It's close to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "fired upon," do you mean with shells, or sniper fire, or both?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Both, both.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement the Praga three-barrel anti-aircraft machine-gun and a multiple rocket-launcher known as the VBR. How did you know the names of these weapons?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those who served in the army told me. I have no experience with it, myself, but that's what they said. And I know they sang that song, "Listen, Alija, how we're firing our Pragas. Not a stone upon stone will remain from you."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was singing these songs?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs, of course. You don't think it's the Muslims, do you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where did you hear these songs being sung?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: They sang that often, even before the war. I heard it on a bus when I travelled from Cajnice to Sarajevo, when I was visiting my father at the hospital in Foca -- in Fojnica, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were injured by a shell on or about the 8th of June, 1992. On the days preceding the day on which you were injured, what was the level of intensity of shelling on those days?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the sniper fired at all times of the day, and the shells were landing also all the time there; day-time, night-time, it didn't matter. At any hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you estimated your village was approximately two or three kilometres away from Sarajevo. What, if anything, did you hear during these days from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard shells falling around the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement that approximately 150 people were being treated when you were admitted to the hospital on the night -- or between the 8th and 9th of June, 1992. Do you know for what types of injuries these people were being treated for?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those were all wounded people, people with major injuries, horrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, what psychological or physical injuries do you suffer from as a result of the shelling and sniping you have described earlier? If you can describe for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm suffering mentally and physically. I'm not well at all. I have all these ticks and traumas from way back then. And when I sleep, I still feel like a shell is falling nearby. And when I dream, it's always in my dreams. I don't know. One has to live with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Mujanovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Ms. Mujanovic, now you'll be asked -- cross-examined by the accused, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Mujanovic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I regret that you had to live through that, and I will try to be brief, as brief as possible. You know what is located in your neighbourhood, don't you? Do you know whether Ugorsko is far away from you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: It isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who populates Ugorsko, predominantly?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly Muslims, but there were Serbs and Croats close to Pretis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the part of Ugorsko that was populated by Muslims, that was under the control of the Muslim Army; right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: A part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Barica; who is the dominant ethnic group populating it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's mixed. There was Serbs living near where I lived. They never left. They still live there to this day, and they were driven out just like our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who is the dominant ethnic group in Barica?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Muslims had a significant majority in Barica? [In English] She doesn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, do you follow us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear. Poorly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the Court Deputy in Sarajevo could turn up the volume. Do you hear me now again? I hope that you now hear us better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note a failure on the part of the transcript as well. Shall we break for 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether the Court Deputy in Sarajevo could hear us. If you can advise Mrs. Mujanovic that we'll have a break for 10 minutes to look into the technical matters. We'll rise now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies, Mrs. Mujanovic, for your inconvenience. I take it now you are able to hear us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: ... your attention for a moment to make things easier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The French translation is over-riding. Yes, please -- does he have to repeat the question? Because we are not following the transcript, I'm not sure whether the court reporter got that. But just in case, could you repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, in order to speed up this, I would like to put to you something about the position of these settlements, and you can tell me if that is correct or incorrect. I'm reading from the 1991 census. There were 2.042 Muslims and 800 Serbs in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In a settlement the interpreters didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't count and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you agree that it was a predominantly Muslim settlement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer this question: The interpreters here in The Hague were not able to hear your previous answer. And, Madam Mujanovic, because Mr. Karadzic's question and your answer should be translated so that -- interpreted so that we can follow, please put a pause between the question and your answer. So could you repeat your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't count the inhabitants. I know that the population was mixed, but I don't know how many were of each group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there a church or a mosque in Hotonj?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were in power, they didn't have them. Now, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who had Kobilja Glava under their control?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Kobilja Glava was under our control, and you held the area up there, Orahov Brijeg, and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who had Hotonj under their control?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You did, for the most part, but I don't know. I wasn't really there. I don't know who held which area, nor am I interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mrs. Mujanovic, you said some important things, both in your statement and in your evidence today, that we need to portray here in an objective light so that we know what it is that you are saying based on your knowledge and what is the impression that you gained from the newspapers or from propaganda or elsewhere. Do you agree that Kobilja Glava had 2.756 Muslims and only 46 Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. To tell you the truth, I don't know. In the old days, we had brotherhood and unity. Nobody paid attention to who was a Muslim and who was a Serb, as long as they were human beings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with you. And it would have been better if it had remained that way, but it didn't. It's different now. Now, would you agree with me that in Vogosca, the Muslim settlements were under the Muslim control and the Serb settlements were under the Serb control? As for Hotonj, Kobilja Glava, Ugorsko, and similar settlements, they were controlled by Muslims, whereas the Serbs controlled Blagovac, Poljine, Krivoglavci, and so on; is that true?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Barica have their own unit of Green Berets and Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are not sure what the witness answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Muslim Army gather in Barica before the attack, and did they return to Barica following their attacks?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mrs. Mujanovic, could you repeat your answer to the question whether there was Green Beret in Barica? The interpreters couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Who would come up with such an idea?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the war, was there any army permanently stationed in the Barica area?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that there were our civilians living there. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said, in your supplemental statement of 13th October, that you were quite afraid because you lived close to the separation line; is that true?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who was separated there? Which armies were separated there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't the armies that were separated, but the residents fled from Vogosca, and they came, saying that Serbs were killing, raping, snatching everything that was there. I was afraid for my safety and the safety of my children, so I fled to Sip, to my sister-in-law's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any Serb trenches there, near Barica?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I, personally, didn't go there to see, but I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Between your village and the Serb trenches, were there any Muslim trenches?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that for a while in April, you went away to get away from the combat; right? So you were not driven out; you went away yourself?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I went away out of fear, because I was afraid that the Serb Army would come along, and God knows what would happen. People came from Vogosca, telling us about what had happened in Vogosca, and Vogosca is not far away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. I will now ask you to look at a map and to specify where your village is located and what can be found in your village and around it. Could we see P1058, please. P1058.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the witness is able to see the map through e-court or she should see the map on hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it can be seen on the screen. We need to zoom into the area above the 11th Vitez Mountain Brigade, "11 BB," et cetera. We need to zoom in quite substantially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, do you see a map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be zoomed in further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, do you see where it says "Barica"? It says "3 BB," and then there's a triangle flag, and then it says "Barica. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic advise what the date of this map is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is much later, but the lines did not change from the beginning of the war until the end, except for the Zuc Hill, where we lost some territory. But in Barica, in this area, the lines didn't move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have difficulty following your point, putting this kind of map to Mrs. Mujanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, in the statement of this witness, it says that it was a civilian settlement and that the Serbs fired for no reason. Based on some documents, I will show you that it's quite the contrary, but just to establish, Hotonj and Barica had staff headquarters, and there were mortars, rocket units, and recoilless guns all around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, on this map - I hope the Court Officer can help you - we can see where it says "Hotonj" and "Barica." We can see two flags there, number 2 and number 3, which stands for the 2nd and for the 3rd Battalion. Do you maintain your position that there was no army in your vicinity?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I maintain that there were only civilian inhabitants there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, do you see this line, dotted line, a blue one and a red one, running near Hotonj? Is this where the separation lines were?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know much about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I fully understand you, but I don't understand, then, why they selected you to testify about military matters. There were troops there, there were rocket units, mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She is testifying as a victim of a shelling incident. She's not a member of the military unit at all. Are you challenging that she was injured by a shelling incident? Then put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm challenging -- Mrs. Mujanovic, I'm challenging the fact that you were wounded in a Serb attack on a civilian settlement. I put to you that you were wounded because you went out with a child in front of the house on the morning when a large Muslim offensive started against Serb positions, Poljine, Kromolj, and all other Serb positions. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, shame on you. You know that shells landed in our settlement, on civilian residents, every day. You know that Muslims did not have any heavy weaponry. You know, yourself, that should a war erupt in Bosnia, the Muslim people would not be able to defend themselves. Shame on you. I'm a civilian. I was never in the military. I was wounded in front of my own house, on my own hearth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. That morning, early in the morning, before you went out, did a large Muslim offensive against Serb positions, against Poljine and the Serb part of Vogosca, start?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We won't deal with that any more. Now let me put another question to you, Mrs. Mujanovic. From the beginning of the war, from the beginning of April, Green Berets attacked the Pretis factory in Vogosca, including Barica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it isn't. It isn't, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now -- we don't need this map anymore. It wasn't of much use, except that I ask all participants to look at this map to see what it looks like. Could we now see 1D2698, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, Mrs. Mujanovic, is a report from the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic, Police Station Ilidza, and it says here that a certain Jovan, which is Jovan Divjak, just after transferring from the JNA to the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, called upon the citizens of Vogosca and the guards of Pretis to defend the installations of Pretis from what was said to be an attack of the Serbian forces from the direction of Ilijas. The said appeal, according to the source, served as a smoke-screen for an action by the Green Berets because it -- because soon afterwards, from the direction of Sarajevo, five trucks arrived at Pretis, including one that the Green Berets had filled with certain equipment, and the others never arrived because, in the meantime, these forces of the Serbian Territorial Defence from Vogosca were activated and skirmished with the Green Berets. Do you know that there was an attack on Pretis by the Muslim forces on the 11th of April?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we adopt this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see a basis to admit this, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting because someone else was speaking. Can we get 1D2696.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll just tell you what this is, Mrs. Mujanovic. This is from a time when the JNA were still in Sarajevo, and this is a letter addressed to Alija Izetbegovic by the Command of the 2nd Military District. And in the first sentence, General Kukanjac informs President Izetbegovic as follows: "In the night between the 17th and 18th of April, 1992, your Green Berets carried out an attack on a part of the factory at Vogosca (Pretis, special purpose that is military industry). You are aware of the outcome of that attack." Do you now feel convinced that an attack took place?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I would very much appreciate it if you didn't ask me such questions. I'm a civilian. I was never involved in anything military or strategic of the kind that you ask me about. I sat at home. I was wounded while at home. I really don't know any of these things and I'm not interested in them. You should ask someone else about that. I know nothing about these attacks, and I have really no answer. I was not a soldier. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but I ask you for some understanding and patience. You were invited here to testify to the effect that Serbs attacked a civilian neighbourhood, whereas I am saying that Barica was a source of constant attacks on the military installations in Vogosca and the surrounding Serbian neighbourhoods. And because you were asked to testify to that position, the Defence has to question that and to put its case that Barica was not a civilian neighbourhood, that it was full of army troops, and that somebody turned Barica into a military target, and that was done by your army.

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Anyone could pass freely through Barica without being stopped by anyone. You could have passed through without being intercepted, without being checked. All I know is a civilian population was there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the witness say anything about this document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this document eminently refutes everything the witness is saying. What am I supposed to do when a witness like this is brought? And it's true that she was wounded. Everything else is not true.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am saying what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mrs. Mujanovic, what did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am saying only what I know. Let me ask me -- let him ask me about things that I know. I have nothing to say about things I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you put your case to the witness. And then you'll have another opportunity to tender this document, which may be admitted, and then all the credibility issues will be raised later on and assessed by the Chamber. You don't have to put each and every document, item, to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic, then I have to take up matters that you've said and to contest them. You never mentioned before that Serbs had expelled the Muslims from wherever. Why are you saying this for the first time now?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody asked me before, but I know that because I also had to leave my home, out of fear, from hearing all the stories of the refugees who are fleeing from thugs carrying guns and knives. All sorts of people passed through, people who were beaten up and wounded. They passed by my door. I opened my door to them, and I had to give them food and help, and eventually I left my home too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To whom did you give food and water? Those were your fighting men?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were not fighting men. There were civilians; women, children, men, from Vogosca, people who were running.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was a Muslim ever driven out of Poljine?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I never went to Poljine. Until the war began, I didn't even know about the existence of Zuc and Poljine. I only learned about them when the shells started falling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One hundred and forty-one Serbs lived in Poljine, and ten Muslims. Was it then a predominantly Serb village?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask for 65 ter 11701. I believe it has a P number. Page 86. This is from a very well-known witness, Mr. Robert Donia. Page 86.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that Muslims had only hunting weapons, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here is what Robert Donia says, who is pro-Muslim: "The ARBiH Army launched another offensive on 8 June 1992, aiming to take four key hilltops within the city: Zuc, north of the Proletarian Brigade thoroughfare in the Serb-proclaimed Rajlovac municipality; Mojmilo and Vrace ..." Et cetera, et cetera. Do you now believe me there was a major offensive on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, I was wounded, and I was taken to hospital. That was between the 8th and the 9th of June. I don't remember anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So now you allow the possibility there was a major Muslim offensive?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a Serb attack on Barica. We were fired at from all possible weapons. Suljo Skoro [phoen] was wounded then, and many people were injured and there was no one to help us. I was wounded, myself, then and then I was taken to hospital, and I don't recall anything further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 1D2322.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that Donia document is not in evidence. I should stand corrected if I'm wrong. Ms. Sutherland, could you take a look. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's not in evidence, then I would tender page 86.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that page will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D855, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Mujanovic, let me put this document to you. This is a report from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it was called then. For your benefit and for other participants who need the interpretation, let me read it. This is from the 8th of June, 1992. Paragraph 1: "In the course of the day, the enemy developed offensive operations -- launched offensive operations from the city towards the outskirts. Particular pressure was exerted on the following axes: Kobilja Glava Zuc, Boljakov Potok Zuc and Han Zuc. The enemy managed to get control of the line north-east of Rajlovac; Brijesko Brdo, Smiljevici, Ugljesici. The attack was stopped. In the afternoon, the attack was carried out also from the direction of Nahorevo towards the Pionirska Dolina and Betanija. The enemy managed to cut through the road at Trebevic in the sector of the Trvi Sumar [phoen]. The attacks on all other parts of the front-line were unsuccessful. Artillery and mortar fire was directed at Vraca and Vojkovici, Nedzarici, Ilidza, Rajlovac, and VP KAG. We expect a strong attack at the airport in the course of the night. "Successful defence is being put up by the forces in the sector of Vraca, Grbavica, Nedzarici, Ilidza, Hadzici, Rakovica and Ilijas. In the course of the day, we had eight dead and sixty-two injured. Two tanks and five APCs are damaged." And finally: "Request: We ask for reinforcement, including officers and air support, on Mojmilo Brdo ..." Et cetera. Do you agree that a civilian population cannot cause such damage and put up such resistance?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why are you asking me these things, Mr. Karadzic? I was at the hospital and I don't remember any of these things. I was wounded on the 8th of June. I was first at hospital and then at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that. I told you that already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you heard from us so many times. Reading out the documents, which the witness cannot confirm, it's just a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you then look at your statement, para 6. It's your statement dated 5 November 2008. I hope it's available over there in the Serbian language. You're probably not going to admit this, this report of the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not this time, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see, in para 6, where you enumerate some places; Zuc, Krivoglavci, Kromolj, Vogosca, Poljine and Tihovici? You mentioned these names; right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Blagovac and Sucura houses, there was a tank by the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that you actually agree with the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps? He mentions those same places, except he mentions them as places from which your army is attacking.

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Right, and the Serb Army was not attacking neighbourhoods and civilians? I can't understand how you can talk like that. Our people, if they were doing anything, they were defending their homes. They were not going up to a mountain in Romanija. They were standing on their own door steps, defending their own homes.
