utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you believe your own web sites, your own people? Do you believe the web site Angry Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What kind of question it is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd like to put to Mrs. Mujanovic what this Muslim web site says about that day, the 8th of June, and the April attacks on the factory. If I'm not allowed to do that, I'll withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mrs. Mujanovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Mujanovic has already said that she knows nothing of what occurred on the 8th of June after she was injured and taken to the hospital, so she can't speak to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there were enough attacks, even before that, where Barica is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe, Mrs. Mujanovic, that attacks originated from Barica and that these troops returned to Barica after their operations?

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what were they supposed to advance with? Bare-handed, or with a hunting rifle against shells and grenades, would you go?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Mujanovic. I will not torture you anymore. I regret that you were wounded. But you have to be angry on your own politicians who wanted the war and who took you to the -- who pushed you to the front-line.

utterances.speaker: FAHRA MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard you also, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say something. Your Excellency, it is not appropriate to torture this woman, who knows nothing. Indeed, she was wounded, but she doesn't know anything, and there is plenty of evidence indicating that this was not a civilian settlement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why don't you go to Ugorsko, sir, to see if there is anything of military and strategic importance there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then that concludes your evidence, Mrs. Mujanovic. Thank you for your taking time to give your testimony here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say a couple of words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The witness may be excused. Thank you, Mrs. Mujanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The only reason for this witness to appear before the Tribunal is because you challenged her evidence and that you wanted to cross-examine her. Once you put your case to the witness, you don't have to put every document to the witness. I think it's -- I take it that strategy now should be clear to you. Yes. What do you like to raise, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In general terms, I wish to say that this trial can go on for 10 years. It is a burden by the ambition of the Prosecution to bury me with a vast quantity because they don't have enough evidence. If they had five good pieces of evidence and five good witnesses, they wouldn't need hundreds. And the Chamber should protect me, personally, and this trial. What does this mean? Who am I fighting against here? Against this poor woman, who was wounded in an offensive that she knows nothing about? I think that the Chamber should order the Prosecution to re-examine their strategy and what they have in their hands, at their disposal. Otherwise, we'll spend the next five years here. If there is such a procedural option, I suggest that the Chamber order them to summarise this and to come up with some really solid evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All I can say at this moment is: Consult your legal advisers. We'll have a break for 20 minutes, and we'll resume at 10 past 4.00, at which time we'll hear the evidence of Mr. Hajir, I take it, Dr. Hajir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Hajir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could kindly take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: During the course of your testimony today, if there's anything inconvenient for you, please let us know. Yes, Ms. Sutherland, it's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. In the meantime, before we begin, there's Dr. Donia's evidence. I was advised it was already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And so then could you tell us the name of the exhibit -- the number of the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Donia report was 65 ter 21894, admitted as Exhibit P973.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the number given separately will be stricken out. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Witness, could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Youssef Mahmoud Hajir. Youssef Hajir, father's name Mahmoud.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're a doctor of medicine; correct?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Hajir, you testified here on two previous occasions, and that was in the trials of Stanislav Galic, in January of 2002, and Momcilo Perisic, in January of 2009; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've provided a number of statements to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In February of this year, you signed an amalgamated statement which contains relevant parts from your earlier statements, testimony, and information provided to the OTP. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I remember that well. I had some corrections, and I think that they were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. We'll get to those in a moment. Mr. Registrar, could 65 ter 22100 be put on the screen, please -- oh, sorry, be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Could you repeat the number again?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And with Your Honour's leave, I'll read a short summary of the witness's written evidence. The witness is a doctor of medicine who lived in Dobrinja near the start of the war. Dobrinja was a small, predominantly residential area at the western end of Sarajevo, toward the airport. During the course of the war, Dobrinja experienced considerable sniping and shelling activity and became an isolated community, cut off from Sarajevo and from general access to electricity, gas, water, food and emergency medical care. Consequently, in May 1992, because of this isolation and the extreme danger to which both ambulance drivers and injured patients were exposed were they to attempt to drive to hospitals located in Sarajevo, Dr. Hajir founded an emergency hospital and ambulant clinic to provide local medical services to the Dobrinja population. Initially, Dr. Hajir was the only surgeon, and conditions at this emergency hospital were very primitive, with operations being performed by candlelight, with inadequate surgery tools and anaesthesia. The hospital finally became fully operational in July 1992 and eventually utilised the services of 125 to 150 staff. Throughout the war, this hospital treated approximately 16.000 persons. Over 5.000 major operations were performed, over half of which were due directly to the armed conflict. Between 85 and 95 per cent of the people treated at the hospital were civilians, including women, children and the elderly. Dr. Hajir states that the Serbs were absolutely targeting civilians. Dr. Hajir describes one shelling event which occurred on the 1st of June, 1993, and which resulted in the death or injury of over 140 persons. He further describes that, despite its status as a hospital, the facility was shelled on a number of occasions, and hospital staff were killed. Dr. Hajir was shot at three times. Dr. Hajir describes how people still carry deep emotional scars and fears as a result of the sniping, shelling and extreme deprivations due to the war, which has resulted in an increased rate of suicide for the Dobrinja population. Finally, by virtue of Dr. Hajir's position at the hospital, he is able to explain record-keeping procedures in the hospital and authenticate medical records, death certificates, photographs and videos related to the circumstances and incidents described above. Your Honour, that completes the brief summary of the witness's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, you describe in paragraphs 48 to 61 of your statement the effects of the war on the inhabitants, and you state that early in the war there was shortages of water, electricity, fuel and food. How did this affect the running of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: We couldn't really call it a hospital at the beginning. The shortages were continuous, and they were especially bad in the beginning. And later on, it got better, once UNPROFOR arrived and various humanitarian agencies. Initially, it wasn't a hospital; it was an out-patient clinic for urgent cases. And it was certainly affected by everything that was happening in daily life; sick people, people who couldn't go into town, and so on. So we had to admit them into the hospital and treat them there. We couldn't really call it a proper hospital. We had no surgical equipment. We did not have tables for anaesthesia. We couldn't transport patients. So we basically had nothing. I performed difficult surgeries with dental equipment because there was no other way of helping people. So it was a low-grade hospital where we only performed the basic things, sometimes with our bare hands, because we didn't have gloves, we didn't have sterile equipment. We had just a small machine for sterilisation that we could use only for minor equipment so that we could at least stop the bleeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At that early time, were you transferring patients to other hospitals around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: It was a difficult decision to transfer a patient in that environment. The environment of Dobrinja, if I can describe it now. From the east, it was Lukavica. From the northern side, there was Mojmilo, where there were APCs and snipers. On another side, there was the Butile Barracks, with huge numbers of vehicles. And from the fourth side, there was the Nedzarici Barracks. Basically, there were three military barracks around, and Mojmilo was equipped with two or three APCs and tanks, so Dobrinja was completely encircled. It was difficult to decide whether to attempt to transfer a patient across Mojmilo Hill by night, under cover of the night, whether it was worth risking the lives of the people who would carry the injured person and maybe lose four or five lives to save one, or was it better to keep the person inside the hospital, inadequate as it was, and try to do something there. I don't know if that answers your question.

I once suggested that all these vehicles be gathered and placed in the museum to see how many bullet holes there were in them. We used up many of them. But the ambulance drivers were really brilliant. They never gave up on their job. They did their best to transport a patient. But to go to Kosevo Hospital or to the military hospital, or, in other words, the state hospital, was very, very risky.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "The Reporter: Mohamed Arapovic and Mustafa Sipovac, caught minutes earlier by a solitary mortar bomb outside the shelter of their homes which they had left for a rare, fatal breath of fresh air. In the 24 hours we stayed in Dobrinja, eight others would suffer a similar fate. In all those --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to -- the video was stopped at 00:10:11.1. I want to turn now to the incident described in paragraphs 41 to 43 of your statement, and this is the incident which occurred during a football-match held at Dobrinja on the 1st of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you just describe for the Chamber what happened that day at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: It was a Muslim holiday, Bajram, a quiet morning. Suddenly, I heard two or three -- and my memory is hazy on this, whether there were two or three shells at once. And then 10 or 15 minutes later, we had a huge influx of injured people. When 150 injured people arrive at one time, not the biggest hospital in the world can deal with it. It's really a disaster, complete chaos. We put up those people in the doctors' rooms, in wards, in corridors. You couldn't pass through all these people. The hospital was packed with all the rooms available, and the morgue was also filled up. The morgue was big enough to receive three or four bodies, and it was packed. First of all, we needed to do a triage of patients and divide them into groups by urgency, and that was when we really proved ourselves to be a great hospital for emergencies. Within a couple of hours, I had seen all the patients, I assigned them numbers by order of urgency and in groups of 10 people in make-shift vehicles, after they were given emergency assistance, like intubation after being hit by a grenade, immobilising a fracture, immediate assistance in cases of injured thorax. We had done all that, and within a couple of hours after -- after they were given immediate assistance, some of them were sent away. We kept 40 patients -- sorry, we sent away 40 patients to other places, and we kept the rest in our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, in paragraph 15 of your statement, you state that around 16.000 people were treated at the hospital, and of this number, you performed approximately 3.000 major operations due to injuries suffered as a result of the conflict. Is this a conservative number?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: You know about these numbers that are mentioned. You would have had to be there to see what it was all like. When you -- then you would have understood it was simply impossible to account for everything. We were an improvised, make-shift hospital. We didn't even have the paper to do the paperwork properly. We had to deal with preparing instruments in the OR, to do everything from setting up the hospital, to deal with all sorts of problems with establishing the hospital. I was, at the same time, the director, the general manager, and the head surgeon. Not a single surgery went without me, in whatever role. It was a huge responsibility. I had to be the overall manager to take care of all the departments; Pediatrics, Psychiatry, decide what to do with psychiatric patients, Traumatology, all the departments, and I, personally, was never satisfied with our records. I don't know why it never worked properly. What needed to be taken from the patient was the place and date of birth, where they were injured, nature of the injury, what was done during the operation. I repeated all that a thousand times to my staff, but I was never quite happy with the protocols they made. They were never quite up to proper hospital standards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think you're saying the reason for this is because of the -- how you were operating at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: You mean what the reason was for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
